newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strike disrupts a third of French oil refineries.
newsitem.headline: Strike disrupts a third of French oil refineries.

text.p: French oil workers struck again on Tuesday but oil firms said unions had failed to carry out their threat to shut down France's oil industry for a day.
Strikers disrupted a third of French refineries in a one-day protest to widen pressure on employers after a bitter dispute crippled France's biggest oil firm, Elf Aquitaine, last week.
Oil majors Shell, British Petroleum, Esso and Total all said they were hit, each having to slow down or halt output at one of their French plants.
Unions had called a national oil industry strike against efforts by oil firms to tackle surplus capacity by cutting jobs.
Unions and employers agree 1,500 jobs are on the line in France over the next year.
"We demand the total withdrawal of all redundancy plans," an official at the Communist-backed CGT union said.
Those plans were highlighted just as the strike got under way on Tuesday, when Royal Dutch/Shell announced it was studying ways of dealing with excess capacity in southeast France.
The region is served by a cluster of competing refineries including Shell's Berre plant near Marseille, where the strike was hitting hardest after starting a day early on Monday.
A Shell official said the Berre refinery's most important activity of distilling crude oil was being suspended and other operations were at a slowdown or a standstill.

Unions said workers at several other plants would decide whether to join the protest later in the day, but around half of France's 13 refineries were unlikely to take part.Those left out of the action were mainly small units.
Oil prices rose last week when the Elf strike shut down a quarter of French capacity but traders said markets were largely unmoved by Tuesday's more modest slowdowns.
Apart from the nine-day strike at Elf, action by the oil industry's own staff has failed to cause it as much misery as a 12-day blockade of fuel depots by striking truckers last month.
Oil companies blame too many refineries, fierce competition to sell petrol from supermarkets and government tax policies for leaving them with no choice but to shed jobs and reorganise.
"We have all these restructuring problems because the industry is going badly in France," a spokeswoman for oil industry association UFIP said.

Multinational oil firms say they have it particularly badly in France because the government encouraged them through taxes to invest in expensive complexes for making unleaded petrol (gasoline) and now wants them to produce even cleaner diesel.
"We invested five billion francs ($1 billion) in unleaded petrol -- now we have to export it," the UFIP official said.

But unions say oil companies are slashing jobs simply to boost profits. Unions also seek the same early retirement rights won by French truckers after a 12-day strike for as many refinery workers as possible.
